lessons.title: What CRM Is and Why Businesses Use It

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real business you've interacted with recently (a gym, a bank, a software vendor) and write two sentences on a specific moment where it was obvious whether they had, or didn't have, a shared record of you. Then list three pieces of customer information a business would lose track of without a CRM, beyond the lesson's own examples.
slots.deliverable: A half-page written reflection: one real, specific moment revealing system-of-record quality, plus a list of three concrete pieces of customer info a CRM-less business would lose.

lessons.title: The Customer Lifecycle: Marketing, Sales, Service

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a company you're a customer of and identify one real moment from each lifecycle stage: how they marketed to you, what the sales process looked like (even if it was just 'add to cart'), and any service interaction you've had since. Write one sentence on what would have gone wrong if that company's service team had no record of you.
slots.deliverable: A 3-part written walkthrough (one short paragraph per stage) for a real company, plus the one-sentence 'what would break' answer.

lessons.title: CRM Data: Accounts, Contacts, Leads and Opportunities

slots.practicalActivity: Think of a recent purchase you made that had a real sales process (a car, enterprise software, a custom service). Identify exactly what would have been the Lead and what would have been the Opportunity in that process. Explain in 1-2 sentences why a business wouldn't want to create a permanent Contact record for every unqualified lead that ever filled out a form.
slots.deliverable: A written mapping of a real purchase onto Lead and Opportunity, plus the 1-2 sentence explanation of why unqualified leads don't become permanent Contacts.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one metric each from marketing (lead volume, conversion rate, cost per lead), sales (win rate, average deal size, sales cycle length, pipeline), and service (case volume, resolution time, CSAT, churn rate). For each of your three chosen metrics, write one sentence on exactly what bad or missing data would do to that number, then explain why pipeline depends on reps keeping their opportunities current, not just creating them once.
slots.deliverable: Three written metric breakdowns (one per department) describing the data-quality failure mode, plus the pipeline/stale-data explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one CRM alternative named in the lesson (HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Zoho CRM, SAP Sales Cloud, or Pipedrive). Spend five minutes on its real public marketing site and note one advertised feature that maps directly to a Chapter 1 concept (lead, opportunity, pipeline). Write two sentences on why a five-person startup and a 50,000-employee enterprise might reasonably choose different CRM platforms despite needing the same four record types.
slots.deliverable: One named competitor platform with its mapped feature, plus the two-sentence startup-vs-enterprise comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one continuous 200-300 word paragraph tracing a single realistic prospect by name through the entire Chapter 1 arc: how they became a Lead, what made them sales-ready for the handoff to sales, how they got converted into an Account, Contact, and Opportunity, which specific metric from Lesson 4 their progress would move, and why a competing CRM platform might model the same journey slightly differently.
slots.deliverable: One 200-300 word written narrative correctly using Lead, Account, Contact, Opportunity, and at least one named metric from this chapter, in the right order.

slots.practicalActivity: Write two sentences explaining why the 'No Software' pitch was a meaningfully different, riskier bet in 1999 than it would be today. Then pick one of the acquisitions named in the lesson (ExactTarget, Demandware, Tableau, or Slack) and note which Salesforce cloud or product line it most likely became part of.
slots.deliverable: The two-sentence 'No Software' explanation, plus the named acquisition and the cloud/product line it maps to.

lessons.title: The Salesforce Clouds: Sales, Service, Marketing, Commerce and Platform

slots.practicalActivity: For each of Sales, Service, Marketing, and Commerce Cloud, write one sentence connecting it back to a specific stage of the Chapter 1 customer lifecycle (marketing, sales, or service). Then explain in your own words why 'Platform' isn't listed alongside the other four as a fifth business-function cloud.
slots.deliverable: Four one-sentence cloud-to-lifecycle mappings, plus a short written explanation of why Platform is categorically different from the four business-function clouds.

lessons.title: The Salesforce Platform vs. Salesforce Applications

slots.practicalActivity: Write one sentence describing something you could build directly on the Salesforce Platform that has nothing to do with selling anything (an equipment-maintenance tracker, an event-registration portal, or similar). Then explain, in your own words, why 'I use Salesforce' alone doesn't tell you whether someone configures a pre-built application or builds new applications on the platform underneath it.
slots.deliverable: The custom-build example sentence, plus the written platform-vs-application explanation distinguishing the admin and developer sides of that split.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free Trailhead account if you don't already have one, browse the real AppExchange marketplace at appexchange.salesforce.com, and find one free listing relevant to a business problem you choose. Note its pricing model, star rating, and review count. Explain why checking reviews and data-access requirements matters before installing anything into a real production org.
slots.deliverable: One real AppExchange listing's name, pricing model, and rating/review count, plus the written data-access-risk explanation.

lessons.title: Salesforce Roles: Admin, Developer, Consultant, Architect

slots.practicalActivity: For each of the four roles (Administrator, Developer, Consultant, Architect), write one sentence on which Chapter 2 concept (clouds, platform-vs-application, AppExchange) connects most directly to that role's day-to-day work. Then explain why a consultant typically works for a partner firm rather than inside the company that's actually using Salesforce.
slots.deliverable: Four role-to-concept sentences, plus the written explanation of why consultants usually sit at partner firms rather than inside the client company.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one short, 200-300 word case study of a hypothetical Salesforce implementation project, naming which of the four roles (admin, developer, consultant, architect) handles which part of the work, which cloud(s) are involved, and whether any piece of the solution comes from an AppExchange listing rather than being built from scratch.
slots.deliverable: One 200-300 word written case study correctly using role, cloud, platform/application, and AppExchange concepts together in one coherent scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Log in to any Salesforce org (a free Trailhead Playground works) and check Setup -> Company Information for your org's Instance name. Visit trust.salesforce.com and search for that instance name to see its current status. Write 1-2 sentences explaining to a non-technical friend why Salesforce can push a new feature to millions of users overnight, tying the answer back to multitenancy.
slots.deliverable: The org's recorded Instance name and its current trust.salesforce.com status, plus the 1-2 sentence multitenancy explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: In your org, go to Setup and search 'Company Information' in Quick Find. Record your org's Edition and Organization ID. Scroll to the User Licenses section and note how many 'Salesforce' licenses are Total vs. Used in your org.
slots.deliverable: A written record of the org's Edition, Organization ID, and the Total/Used count for the Salesforce license type.

slots.practicalActivity: In Setup, go to Object Manager -> Account -> Fields & Relationships, and find the standard 'Industry' field, noting its picklist values (that field's definition is metadata). Create a Contact record for a real-sounding person (that record is data). Write one sentence explaining why a Flow you build with clicks in Setup doesn't require a developer to 'compile' anything.
slots.deliverable: The Industry field's picklist values, one created Contact record, and the one-sentence metadata/Flow explanation.

lessons.title: Release Cycles: Three Releases a Year

slots.practicalActivity: Search 'Salesforce release notes' for the current release and skim the table of contents for one cloud (e.g. Sales Cloud). Find one feature explicitly listed as 'opt-in', note what it does and why an admin might choose to delay enabling it, then check trust.salesforce.com for your org's instance's next scheduled maintenance window.
slots.deliverable: One named opt-in feature with its description and delay rationale, plus the instance's next scheduled maintenance window date.

lessons.title: Trust, Availability and Salesforce Security Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Go to trust.salesforce.com and search for your org's instance (from the multitenancy lesson). Note its current status. Click into the Security tab and find one published security advisory or best-practice document. In your org's Setup, go to Users and find your own user record, noting which Profile you're assigned.
slots.deliverable: The instance's current status, one named security advisory or document, and your assigned Profile name.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same org, write one combined 'org health check' report pulling together this entire chapter: the org's Edition and Instance, one real piece of metadata and one real piece of data you can point to in the org, the org's current release name, and its trust.salesforce.com status alongside your own Profile.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated written org health-check report covering real, specific data points from your own org for all five How Salesforce Works lessons.

slots.practicalActivity: Explain in plain language, as if to a new hire on their first day, why Salesforce can run two unrelated companies on the exact same servers without either seeing the other's data, why that same architecture is what lets a 30-second Setup click create a new field without a developer, and why 'what release and instance are we on' is a normal admin question rather than a sign something is wrong.
slots.deliverable: One 250-350 word written 'first day' explanation connecting multitenancy, metadata, and release cycles into a single coherent story.

slots.practicalActivity: In your org, click the Accounts tab and open any record. Identify three fields on that record. In Setup -> Object Manager, scroll the full object list and count how many objects have a label ending in '__c' (custom objects). Write one sentence explaining the difference between a record and a field to someone who has never used Salesforce.
slots.deliverable: The three identified fields, the custom-object count from Object Manager, and the one-sentence record-vs-field explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: In your org, click the App Launcher and note at least three apps listed. Switch into a different app than the one you started in, and notice which tabs changed. Use the App Launcher's search box to find an object that isn't visible in your current app's tab bar at all.
slots.deliverable: The three listed apps, a note on which tabs changed after switching apps, and the object you found via search that wasn't in the original app's tab bar.

lessons.title: Navigating the Home Page, Tabs and List Views

slots.practicalActivity: Open the Opportunities (or any object) tab and note the name of the default list view shown. Use the list view picker to switch to a different saved list view. Create a new list view filtered to just your own records, and save it.
slots.deliverable: The default list view's name, the alternate list view you switched to, and your newly created, saved 'My Records' list view.

slots.practicalActivity: Without looking back at the glossary tables, write down definitions for five terms from memory, then check your answers against the lesson. Pick the two terms you find most similar-sounding or easiest to confuse (such as 'object' vs. 'app', or 'profile' vs. 'permission set'), and write one sentence each explaining the difference.
slots.deliverable: The five self-tested term definitions plus the two disambiguation sentences for the most easily confused terms.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real or imagined business. In a few sentences, describe how its Marketing, Sales, and Service teams might each use a different Salesforce app, but share the same underlying Account records. Name one industry-specific way a company outside typical B2B sales (a nonprofit or university) might adapt Salesforce's standard objects to its own needs.
slots.deliverable: The department/app write-up showing three apps sharing one Account, plus the named industry-specific standard-object adaptation.

slots.practicalActivity: In your own org, build one end-to-end 'day in the life' walkthrough: switch into the Sales app and create one Opportunity tied to a new Account and Contact, build a filtered list view showing just that Opportunity, then switch into a different app and confirm the same Account record is still reachable from there — proving hands-on that apps are different surfaces on one shared org.
slots.deliverable: One documented walkthrough (notes or screenshots) showing the same Account visible from two different apps, plus the filtered list view you built along the way.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page 'readiness check' for the next course, Hands-On Salesforce Environment: using this course's glossary, define in your own words Org, Edition, Metadata, App, and List View, and name one open question you still have about navigating Setup that you expect the next course to answer.
slots.deliverable: A one-page readiness-check document with five self-written definitions and one open Setup question carried forward into the next course.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can explain what CRM is, navigate Salesforce's clouds/platform/role ecosystem, describe how a real org actually runs (multitenancy, editions, licenses, metadata, releases), and move confidently around Setup, apps, tabs, and list views in their own Salesforce org.
